title: Count the Work Done. Not Just the Cores. Intel.
gist: Intel argues agentic-AI infrastructure should be benchmarked on 'delivered agents per rack' rather than core count, citing data showing CPU scheduling overhead rises to 15% of latency at 32 concurrent agent requests and GPUs sit idle 40-50% of the time, while pointing to Xeon 6 Flat Memory Mode, IAA offload and its upcoming Crescent Island GPU as its answer.

themes.theme: Reframing the Metric: Delivered Work, Not Core Count

insights.claim: The right way to evaluate CPU infrastructure for agentic AI is not raw core count or single-thread speed, but how much useful agent work the system reliably completes within the latency, cost and power limits a business requires.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Signals how Intel wants to reframe competitive benchmarking for AI infrastructure — watch for this metric appearing in future Intel marketing and guidance versus AMD EPYC or ARM server chip comparisons.
insights.quote: How much useful agent work can my infrastructure reliably complete within the latency, cost and power limits my business requires?
insights.locator: The debate about CPUs for Agentic AI

insights.claim: A single agent loop makes performance look straightforward — finish each step faster and the workflow moves faster — but production systems run many agents at once competing for CPU, memory, I/O and accelerator resources, which shifts the bottleneck from single-thread speed to system-level resource contention.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A key mental model for evaluating CPU/GPU sizing decisions for agent fleets: single-thread benchmarks are misleading for real production deployments.

insights.claim: In a public analysis of 739 anonymized Claude Code conversations (multi-turn coding-agent workflows with tool use), CPU-side processing and wait time rose from under 1% of total latency for a single request to as much as 15% at 32 concurrent requests, with most of the increase coming from scheduling and queueing rather than computation.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that CPU scheduling and queueing, not raw compute, become the dominant latency driver at production-scale agent concurrency — supports demand for smarter orchestration silicon over simply adding cores.
insights.locator: In a recent public analysis using 739 anonymized Claude Code conversations

insights.claim: The same research estimates that for code-execution agents, GPUs perform useful work during only 50% to 60% of wall-clock time, because when an agent waits for a database, retrieval system or sandbox, the GPU waits too.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Real-world GPU utilization in agentic AI deployments may run well below theoretical peak — a material input for modeling GPU fleet ROI and hyperscaler capex efficiency.
insights.quote: The most expensive accelerator is the one waiting for the rest of the system.
insights.locator: Waiting also reaches the most expensive part of the system

insights.claim: Intel proposes the formula Delivered Agents per Rack = Theoretical Agents per Rack x Routing Efficiency x Resource Balance x Offload Efficiency to quantify real agent throughput versus theoretical capacity.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Gives investors and buyers a structured framework to press vendors, including Intel, for apples-to-apples agentic-AI infrastructure benchmarks rather than accepting peak-throughput marketing numbers.
insights.locator: One way to understand delivered capacity is

insights.claim: In a joint Intel and SAP evaluation, Xeon 6 Flat Memory Mode — which combines CXL-attached memory and native DDR5 in one address space — delivered 96% of all-DDR5 performance at roughly 25% lower memory total cost of ownership.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A concrete, third-party-validated TCO number for CXL memory expansion, relevant for evaluating Intel's memory-tiering pitch against competitors and broader CXL ecosystem momentum.

insights.claim: Intel QuickAssist Technology, Data Streaming Accelerator and In-Memory Analytics Accelerator (IAA) offload infrastructure work that would otherwise consume general-purpose cores; published work using IAA for snapshot compression delivered approximately 1.2x faster snapshot completions.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Quantifies one concrete efficiency gain from Intel's built-in fixed-function accelerators, a differentiator versus competitors lacking similar offload silicon, though the cited 1.2x figure is modest.

insights.claim: Bandwidth keeps an agent moving while memory capacity keeps it from starting a session over, which is the rationale Intel gives for combining CXL-attached memory with DDR5 to keep more agent sessions warm at lower cost.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Ties memory-capacity economics directly to agent session continuity and cost, relevant for evaluating memory-tiering vendors and CXL adoption drivers beyond Intel specifically.

insights.claim: The Xeon portfolio spans high per-thread P-core performance and dense E-core throughput on a common architecture, letting the system place each agentic workflow phase — orchestration, tool execution, data services, state movement — on the execution profile best suited to it.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A hybrid P-core/E-core architecture is pitched as a specific agentic-AI advantage, worth comparing against AMD's and ARM vendors' core-mix strategies for the same workloads.
insights.locator: Match the resource to the job

insights.claim: Intel is preparing a Crescent Island GPU aimed at agentic workloads, positioned alongside Xeon CPUs so accelerators are not left idle waiting on the rest of the system.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Confirms Intel is building its own GPU for agentic AI rather than ceding the accelerator market to Nvidia and AMD entirely — a concrete product to track in Intel's AI hardware roadmap.

insights.claim: Intel intends to report agents per rack at a stated p99 latency target on real agentic traces, along with routing efficiency, gains from fixed-function offload, host efficiency in GPU-attached systems, and agents per watt under a defined rack power constraint.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A benchmarking commitment investors and customers can hold Intel accountable to in future disclosures, and a bid to set the industry-standard agentic-AI metric before competitors do.
insights.locator: Intel intends to report agents per rack

insights.claim: Every agentic AI performance claim, including Intel's own, should state the concurrency level, the latency target, and the losses between theoretical and delivered capacity — otherwise the result describes potential, not production capacity.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A call for skepticism toward vendor peak-performance marketing across the whole industry, useful as a lens for evaluating any AI infrastructure vendor's benchmark claims, not just Intel's.
insights.quote: a result describes potential, not production capacity
